summary.text: Count, over all vertex permutations with a distinguished first vertex, neighbor-ending prefixes that support a rooted copy of the tree; induction on the tree uses a first-qualifying-prefix rotation to glue branches at a nonleaf root, and a block-reversal injection after deleting a leaf, losing at most one state per permutation, to obtain at most \((t-2)n!\) excess marked states over rooted-copy states. If the tree is absent the latter vanish, while the marked states number exactly \(2|E(G)|(n-1)!\), so cancellation gives \(2|E(G)|\le (t-2)n=(k-1)n\), contradicting the assumed density.

full_proof.text:
We prove the stated assertion. Throughout, “a copy of a graph \(H\) in a graph \(G\)” means an injective map from \(V(H)\) to \(V(G)\) which sends every edge of \(H\) to an edge of \(G\). The copy need not be induced.

The main ingredient is the following tree-free edge bound.

**Tree-free edge bound.** Let \(T\) be a tree with \(t\ge 2\) vertices, and let \(G\) be a nonempty finite graph with \(N\) vertices. If \(G\) contains no copy of \(T\), then
\[
        2e(G)\le (t-2)N.                                      \tag{1}
\]

We establish this bound by counting marked cuts in permutation words.

Fix, for the moment, a list \(L\) of all vertices of \(G\), with no repetitions. A full word is a permutation
\[
        b,q_1,q_2,\ldots,q_{N-1}
\]
of \(L\). We regard \(b\) as a distinguished root image and \(q_1,\ldots,q_{N-1}\) as the outer word. For \(1\le i\le N-1\), the cut after \(q_i\) is called marked if \(bq_i\in E(G)\). Its displayed outer set is
\[
        X_i=\{q_1,\ldots,q_i\}.
\]

If \(S\) is a graph with a distinguished vertex \(r\), say that this marked cut supports a rooted copy of \((S,r)\) if there is a copy \(f:S\hookrightarrow G\) such that
\[
        f(r)=b,
        \qquad
        f(V(S))\subseteq \{b\}\cup X_i.
\]
Let \(C(S,r)\) be the number of marked cuts, over all full words, which support such a rooted copy. Let \(F\) denote the number of all marked cuts, without any copy condition, and let
\[
        P=N!
\]
be the number of full words.

We will prove, for every rooted tree \((T,r)\) of order \(t\ge2\), that
\[
        F\le C(T,r)+(t-2)P.                                   \tag{2}
\]
The proof requires two finite counting inequalities.

### 1. The marked-word gluing inequality

It is useful first to formulate a general word operation. Fix a root \(b\), and consider all permutations of the other \(N-1\) vertices. Suppose \(A,B,C\) are properties of displayed outer sets, with the following two features:

1. whenever \(C(X)\) holds, \(A(X)\) holds;
2. if \(R\cap X=\varnothing\), \(A(R)\) holds, and \(B(X)\) holds, then \(C(R\cup X)\) holds.

For each property, count the cuts whose last displayed letter is adjacent to \(b\) and whose displayed set has that property. Also declare the cut at position \(0\) to be “allowed,” even though it has no last letter. Then
\[
 \#A+\#B\le \#\{\text{all marked cuts}\}
       +\#\{\text{outer words}\}+\#C.                         \tag{3}
\]

Here is the injection proving this inequality. It is enough to inject the \(A\)-cuts which are not \(C\)-cuts into the allowed cuts which are not \(B\)-cuts. Take such an \(A\)-cut at position \(k\) in a repetition-free word \(l\). Among the prefixes of length at most \(k\), choose the first prefix \(r\) which is marked, has property \(A\), and does not have property \(C\). Such a prefix exists because the whole prefix at the original cut has these properties. Write
\[
        l=(r x)y,
        \qquad |r|+|x|=k.
\]
Thus \(rx\) is the original displayed prefix. Rotate the two initial blocks and replace the cut by the cut after \(x\):
\[
        (r x)y\longmapsto x(r y),
        \qquad k\longmapsto |x|.                              \tag{4}
\]
The new word is a permutation of the old one. If \(x\ne\varnothing\), its last letter is the last letter of the original prefix \(rx\), so the new cut is marked. If \(x=\varnothing\), it is the specially allowed zero cut. Thus the image is always an allowed cut.

Moreover, the displayed sets of \(r\) and \(x\) are disjoint, because the word has no repeated letters. If the new cut had property \(B\), then property \(A\) for \(r\), property \(B\) for \(x\), and the gluing assumption would imply property \(C\) for the union, which is exactly the displayed set of the original prefix \(rx\). This contradicts the choice of the original cut. Hence the new cut does not have property \(B\).

The operation is injective on the cuts under consideration. Indeed, the output records both the rotated word \(xry\) and \(|x|\), so it determines \(x\) and the remaining suffix \(ry\). Inside that suffix, \(r\) is characterized as its first prefix which is marked, has property \(A\), and fails property \(C\). Therefore \(r\), and then \(y\), are uniquely determined. Rotating back recovers the original word and cut.

Consequently
\[
        \#(A\setminus C)\le \#(\text{allowed}\setminus B).
\]
Since every \(C\)-cut is an \(A\)-cut, and the allowed cuts consist disjointly of all marked cuts together with one zero cut for every outer word, rearrangement gives (3).

Now sum (3) over all choices of the first letter \(b\). The number of outer words with first letter \(b\) is \((N-1)!\), and summing over the \(N\) choices of \(b\) gives \(N!=P\). Thus the root-dependent version is
\[
        C_A+C_B\le F+P+C_C,                                   \tag{5}
\]
whenever rooted families \(A,B,C\) have the restriction and gluing properties just described.

We apply this when a rooted tree is split into two branches meeting only at their common root. More precisely, let \(T\) be rooted at \(r\), and let \(A\subseteq V(T)\) contain \(r\). Suppose every edge from \(A\) to its complement has its endpoint in \(A\) equal to \(r\). Put
\[
        T_1=T[A],
        \qquad
        T_2=T[A^c\cup\{r\}],

the two induced rooted subgraphs, both rooted at \(r\). A rooted copy of \(T\) supported on a displayed set restricts to a rooted copy of \(T_1\), so the first condition above is satisfied.

Conversely, suppose a cut supported a rooted copy of \(T_1\) on an outer set \(R\), and another cut supported a rooted copy of \(T_2\) on a disjoint outer set \(X\), with both roots mapped to the same vertex \(b\). These two copies glue to a copy of \(T\). Within either branch injectivity is already known. An image from the first branch other than \(b\) lies in \(R\), while an image from the second branch other than \(b\) lies in \(X\); disjointness prevents a collision between the two branches. Edges internal to a branch are preserved by the corresponding copy. Any edge crossing the partition is incident with \(r\), by assumption, and therefore belongs to the second rooted branch as well; it too is preserved. Hence (5) gives
\[
 C(T_1,r)+C(T_2,r)\le F+P+C(T,r).                              \tag{6}
\]

### 2. Moving the root to a newly attached leaf

Let \(S\) be any graph rooted at \(r\), and let \(S^+\) be obtained by attaching one new leaf \(u\) to \(r\). Root \(S^+\) at the new leaf \(u\). Then
\[
        C(S,r)\le C(S^+,u)+P.                                 \tag{7}
\]

To prove this, fix a full word and order its cuts which support a rooted copy of \((S,r)\). Discard, if it exists, the first such cut. This loses at most one state per full word, hence at most \(P\) states in total. We inject every remaining state into one counted by \(C(S^+,u)\).

Take a remaining state at cut \(k\), and choose an earlier supporting cut \(j<k\) in the same word. Write the word as
\[
        b,p,w,z,

after inserting commas only to indicate blocks, where \(p=q_1\cdots q_{k-1}\), \(w=q_k\), and \(z\) is the remaining suffix. Since the cut at \(k\) is marked, \(bw\in E(G)\). The rooted copy of \(S\) supplied by the earlier cut at \(j\) has root image \(b\) and all its other images among the first \(j\) letters of \(p\). In particular \(w\) is not in the image of this copy: all letters in the word are distinct, and also \(w\ne b\) because \(bw\) is an edge in a simple graph.

We may therefore extend the copy of \(S\) by sending the new leaf \(u\) to \(w\). Injectivity is preserved, and the new leaf edge is sent to the edge \(wb\).

Now transform the full word by reversing both blocks at the cut just after \(w\):
\[
        b,p,w,z\longmapsto w,p^{\mathrm{rev}},b,z^{\mathrm{rev}}. \tag{8}
\]
Keep the numerical cut \(k\), now viewed in the outer word following the new first letter \(w\). Its displayed prefix is
\[
        p^{\mathrm{rev}},b.
\]
It ends in \(b\), which is adjacent to the new root image \(w\). It also supports the extended copy: the new root \(u\) maps to \(w\), the old root maps to \(b\), and all other old images occurred in an initial part of \(p\), hence are among the letters of \(p^{\mathrm{rev}}\).

The operation (8), with the cut retained, is an involution: reverse the initial block through the cut and reverse the remaining block once more, and the original word returns. It is therefore injective. This proves (7).

### 3. The rooted tree inequality

We now prove (2) by induction on \(t=|V(T)|\), simultaneously for every choice of root \(r\).

If \(t=2\), every marked cut itself supports a rooted copy of \(T\). Indeed, let the first letter be \(b\), and let the last letter of the displayed prefix be \(w\), so \(bw\in E(G)\). Map the chosen root of \(T\) to \(b\) and its other vertex to \(w\). The map is injective because \(b\ne w\), and every possible edge of a simple graph on two vertices is sent to \(bw\). Therefore
\[
        F\le C(T,r),
\]
which is (2) because \(t-2=0\).

Assume now \(t\ge3\), and that (2) is known for all smaller trees of order at least two. Since \(T\) is connected and has more than one vertex, the root \(r\) has a neighbor; choose one and call it \(s\).

First suppose \(r\) is a leaf, so \(s\) is its unique neighbor. Delete \(r\), and call the resulting tree \(S=T-r\), rooted at \(s\). Deleting a leaf from a tree leaves a connected acyclic graph, hence a tree, and \(|V(S)|=t-1\ge2\). By induction,
\[
        F\le C(S,s)+(t-3)P.
\]
The original rooted tree \((T,r)\) is precisely \(S\) with one leaf attached at \(s\), rooted at that new leaf. Applying (7) gives
\[
        C(S,s)\le C(T,r)+P.
\]
Combining the two inequalities yields
\[
        F\le C(T,r)+(t-2)P,
\]
as required.

It remains to consider the case in which \(r\) is not a leaf. Then, besides \(s\), it has another neighbor \(z\ne s\). Remove the edge \(rs\) from \(T\), and let \(A\) be the vertex set of the component containing \(r\). Because every edge of a tree is a bridge, \(s\notin A\), and the only edge between \(A\) and its complement is \(rs\). Also \(z\in A\): otherwise both \(rs\) and \(rz\) would cross from the component \(A\), contradicting that the removed edge \(rs\) is the only possible crossing edge.

The induced graph
\[
        T_1=T[A]
\]
is a tree. The graph
\[
        T_2=T[A^c\cup\{r\}]
\]
is also a tree: \(T[A^c]\) is the other component created by deleting \(rs\), and adding \(r\) and the edge \(rs\) attaches one leaf to that component. Both are rooted at \(r\). If
\[
        a=|A|,
        \qquad b=|A^c\cup\{r\}|,
\]
then \(r,z\in A\), so \(a\ge2\), while \(r,s\in A^c\cup\{r\}\), so \(b\ge2\). Each is smaller than \(t\): the first omits \(s\), and the second omits \(z\). Finally the two vertex sets cover \(V(T)\) and overlap exactly at \(r\), so
\[
        a+b=t+1.                                               \tag{9}
\]

Apply the inductive hypothesis separately to \(T_1\) and \(T_2\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
        F&\le C(T_1,r)+(a-2)P,\\
        F&\le C(T_2,r)+(b-2)P.
\end{aligned}
\]
Adding and then using the branch-gluing inequality (6), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
        2F
        &\le C(T_1,r)+C(T_2,r)+(a+b-4)P\\
        &\le F+P+C(T,r)+(a+b-4)P\\
        &=F+C(T,r)+(t-2)P,
\end{aligned}

the last equality following from (9). Subtracting \(F\) proves (2). This completes the induction.

### 4. Counting all marked states

We now evaluate \(F\) exactly. Fix the first letter \(b\). There are \((N-1)!\) permutations of the remaining vertices. In each such outer word, marked cuts correspond exactly to neighbors of \(b\): a neighbor \(w\) occurs in one unique position, and the cut at that position is marked. Thus, for fixed \(b\), the number of marked states is
\[
        (N-1)!\deg_G(b).
\]
Summing over all \(b\in V(G)\) and using the degree-sum formula gives
\[
        F=(N-1)!\sum_b\deg_G(b)
         =(N-1)!\,2e(G).                                      \tag{10}
\]
Also \(P=N!=N(N-1)!\).

If \(G\) contains no copy of \(T\), then no marked cut can support a rooted copy of \(T\), so \(C(T,r)=0\). Substituting this and (10) into (2) gives
\[
        (N-1)!\,2e(G)\le (t-2)N! 
        =(t-2)N(N-1)!.
\]
Because \(N>0\), the factorial \((N-1)!\) is positive and can be cancelled. We obtain
\[
        2e(G)\le (t-2)N,
\]
which proves the tree-free edge bound (1).

### 5. Application to the stated density

Let \(n,k\in\mathbb N\) satisfy \(k+1\le n\), let \(G\) be a graph on \(n\) vertices, and suppose
\[
        \frac{k-1}{2}n+1\le e(G),                              \tag{11}
\]
where the arithmetic in (11) is rational. Let \(T\) be any tree on \(k+1\) vertices.

First consider \(k=0\). Then \(T\) has one vertex. Since \(1=k+1\le n\), the host graph has at least one vertex. Sending the unique vertex of \(T\) to any vertex of \(G\) gives an injective edge-preserving map; there are no target edges to check. Thus \(T\) is contained in \(G\).

Now suppose \(k\ge1\). Then \(T\) has
\[
        t=k+1\ge2
\]
vertices, and \(n>0\). If, for contradiction, \(G\) contained no copy of \(T\), the tree-free edge bound would give
\[
        2e(G)\le (t-2)n=(k-1)n.                               \tag{12}
\]
On the other hand, multiplying (11) by \(2\) gives
\[
        2e(G)\ge (k-1)n+2,                                    \tag{13}
\]
which contradicts (12). Hence \(G\) contains a copy of \(T\).

Since \(T\) was arbitrary, every graph satisfying the stated edge lower bound contains every tree on \(k+1\) vertices, as claimed.
